title: Der gestohlene Heller
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 154. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved (gieng, Thür, saß).
about: KHM 154 is a quiet ghost story: a pale, silent child appears at midday for three days running, visible only to a guest at the table, and is finally traced to two small coins — a Heller apiece, the smallest coin there was — that it had kept back from its mother's alms and hidden before it died. Once the parents give the money to a poor man, the child is at rest and never seen again; the haunting turns out to be nothing more than an unfinished errand of conscience.

sentences.t: Es saß einmal ein Vater mit seiner Frau und seinen Kindern Mittags am Tisch,
sentences.l: There sat once a father with his wife and his children at midday at the table,
sentences.i: A father once sat at table at midday with his wife and his children,
sentences.n: “Mittags” is an adverbial genitive — at midday — the same -s that makes nachts and abends. Midday is the hour the tale turns on, and it is set in the first line.

sentences.t: und ein guter Freund, der zum Besuch gekommen war, aß mit ihnen.
sentences.l: and a good friend, who had come for a visit, ate with them.
sentences.i: and a good friend who had come to visit was eating with them.
sentences.n: “zum Besuch” = on a visit. From here on this friend is “der Fremde,” the stranger — the outsider at the table, and the only one who will see anything.

sentences.t: Und wie sie so saßen, und es zwölf Uhr schlug, da sah der Fremde die Thür aufgehen und ein schneeweiß gekleidetes, ganz blasses Kindlein hereinkommen.
sentences.l: And as they sat so, and it struck twelve o’clock, then the stranger saw the door open and a snow-white clothed, quite pale little-child come in.
sentences.i: And as they sat there, and the clock struck twelve, the stranger saw the door open and a little child come in, dressed in snow-white and quite pale.
sentences.n: “sah … aufgehen … hereinkommen” — sehen takes bare infinitives, and both of them wait until the end of the sentence. “aufgehen” here is a door opening, not anything going up in flames. “Kindlein,” like every -lein diminutive, is grammatically neuter, so the tale calls the child “es” throughout.

sentences.t: Es blickte sich nicht um und sprach auch nichts, sondern gieng geradezu in die Kammer neben an.
sentences.l: It did not look around itself and said nothing either, but rather went straight into the chamber next door.
sentences.i: It did not look about it and said nothing at all, but went straight into the next room.
sentences.n: “blickte sich … um” is sich umblicken, split apart. “neben an” stands as two words where modern German writes nebenan, ‘next door.’ “gieng” is the 1857 spelling of ging.

sentences.t: Bald darauf kam es zurück und gieng eben so still wieder zur Thüre hinaus.
sentences.l: Soon thereafter it came back and went just as quietly out through the door again.
sentences.i: Soon afterwards it came back and went out at the door again, just as quietly.
sentences.n: “zur Thüre hinaus” marks the direction twice, once with the preposition and once with “hinaus”; English does it with a single ‘out at.’ “Thüre” is the 1857 spelling of Türe.

sentences.t: Am zweiten und am dritten Tag kam es auf eben diese Weise.
sentences.l: On the second and on the third day it came in just this same way.
sentences.i: On the second day and the third it came in exactly the same way.
sentences.n: “auf diese Weise” = in this way, and “eben” sharpens it to ‘exactly, just.’ Threefold repetition is the ordinary rhythm of these tales; here it is what finally makes the stranger ask.

sentences.t: Da fragte endlich der Fremde den Vater wem das schöne Kind gehörte das alle Mittag in die Kammer gienge.
sentences.l: Then the stranger finally asked the father whose the beautiful child was that went into the chamber every midday.
sentences.i: At last the stranger asked the father whose the lovely child was that went into the chamber every noon.
sentences.n: “wem … gehörte” is literally ‘to whom it belonged’ — the ordinary German way of asking whose a child is. “gienge” is subjunctive, marking the words as the stranger’s report rather than the narrator’s own account; “alle Mittag” = every midday.

sentences.t: „Ich habe es nicht gesehen,“ antwortete er, „und wüßte auch nicht wem es gehören könnte.“
sentences.l: “I have not seen it,” he answered, “and would not know either to whom it could belong.”
sentences.i: “I have not seen it,” he answered, “and I could not say whose it would be.”
sentences.n: “wüßte” is the subjunctive of wissen used to soften an answer — ‘I would not know,’ where English says ‘I could not say.’ It is the 1857 spelling of wüsste.

sentences.t: Am andern Tage, wie es wieder kam, zeigte es der Fremde dem Vater, der sah es aber nicht,
sentences.l: On the other day, when it came again, the stranger showed it to the father, but he did not see it,
sentences.i: The next day, when it came again, the stranger pointed it out to the father, but the father did not see it,
sentences.n: “am andern Tage” is ‘the next day’; ander in this older use means ‘the second, the following.’ The word order in “zeigte es der Fremde dem Vater” repays a second look: the stranger is the subject and “es,” the child, the object, though the object comes first.

sentences.t: und die Mutter und die Kinder alle sahen auch nichts.
sentences.l: and the mother and the children all saw nothing either.
sentences.n: “auch nichts” after a negative is ‘nothing either.’ Only the outsider sees the child, and the tale never explains why.

sentences.t: Nun stand der Fremde auf, gieng zur Kammerthüre, öffnete sie ein wenig und schaute hinein.
sentences.l: Now the stranger stood up, went to the chamber-door, opened it a little and looked in.
sentences.i: So the stranger got up, went to the chamber door, opened it a little way and looked in.
sentences.n: “stand … auf” is aufstehen, split around the subject. Four verbs run on without a conjunction until the last — the plain pace this tale keeps throughout.

sentences.t: Da sah er das Kind auf der Erde sitzen und emsig mit den Fingern in den Dielenritzen graben und wühlen;
sentences.l: Then he saw the child sitting on the ground and busily digging and burrowing with its fingers in the floorboard-cracks;
sentences.i: Then he saw the child sitting on the floor, busily digging and rooting with its fingers in the cracks between the boards;
sentences.n: “graben” here is the verb, to dig — not the noun der Graben, a ditch. “Dielenritzen” is Diele ‘floorboard’ plus Ritze ‘crack’: the gaps between the boards of a plank floor, where a small coin would fall.

sentences.t: wie es aber den Fremden bemerkte, verschwand es.
sentences.l: but when it noticed the stranger, it vanished.
sentences.i: but the moment it noticed the stranger, it was gone.
sentences.n: “wie” again in the sense ‘when, as soon as.’

sentences.t: Nun erzählte er was er gesehen hatte und beschrieb das Kind genau,
sentences.l: Now he told what he had seen and described the child exactly,
sentences.i: Then he told what he had seen and described the child closely,
sentences.n: German leaves out the demonstrative English wants: “erzählte was er gesehen hatte” is ‘told what he had seen,’ with no ‘that which’ to hold the clause.

sentences.t: da erkannte es die Mutter und sagte „ach, das ist mein liebes Kind, das vor vier Wochen gestorben ist.“
sentences.l: then the mother recognised it and said “oh, that is my dear child, that died four weeks ago.”
sentences.i: then the mother knew it, and said, “Oh, that is my dear child, who died four weeks ago.”
sentences.n: “vor vier Wochen” — vor with a stretch of time means ‘ago.’ Nothing until this line has hinted that a child of the house had died.

sentences.t: Sie brachen die Dielen auf und fanden zwei Heller,
sentences.l: They broke the floorboards up and found two Heller,
sentences.i: They prised the floorboards up and found two Heller,
sentences.n: “brachen … auf” is aufbrechen, to break open or prise up. A Heller was the smallest copper coin in circulation; two of them are worth almost nothing, and that is the point of the tale.

sentences.t: die hatte einmal das Kind von der Mutter erhalten, um sie einem armen Manne zu geben,
sentences.l: these the child had once received from the mother, in order to give them to a poor man,
sentences.i: the child had once had them from its mother, to give to a poor man,
sentences.n: The clause opens with the relative “die” standing first for weight — ‘these the child had received.’ “um … zu geben” = in order to give.

sentences.t: es hatte aber gedacht „dafür kannst du dir einen Zwieback kaufen,“ die Heller behalten und in die Dielenritzen versteckt;
sentences.l: but it had thought “for that you can buy yourself a rusk,” kept the Heller and hidden them in the floorboard-cracks;
sentences.i: but it had thought, “You can buy yourself a rusk with that,” and had kept the Heller and hidden them in the cracks of the floor;
sentences.n: The child speaks to itself as “du,” exactly as English thinking-to-oneself says ‘you.’ Three past participles hang on the single “hatte”: gedacht, behalten, versteckt. A Zwieback is twice-baked bread, a rusk.

sentences.t: und da hatte es im Grabe keine Ruhe gehabt, und war alle Mittage gekommen um nach den Hellern zu suchen.
sentences.l: and so it had had no rest in the grave, and had come every midday to search for the Heller.
sentences.i: and so it had had no peace in the grave, and had come back every noon to look for the Heller.
sentences.n: “im Grabe” keeps the old dative -e. “nach etwas suchen” takes nach where English simply says ‘look for.’ The tale states the belief without comment: a small theft left unrighted holds the dead.

sentences.t: Die Eltern gaben darauf das Geld einem Armen, und nachher ist das Kind nicht wieder gesehen worden.
sentences.l: The parents thereupon gave the money to a poor man, and afterwards the child has not been seen again.
sentences.i: The parents thereupon gave the money to a poor man, and after that the child was never seen again.
sentences.n: “einem Armen” is the adjective arm used as a noun, ‘a poor man.’ The closing verb is a perfect passive, “ist … gesehen worden,” which reaches out of the tale into the reader’s own present.

glossary.aufgehen: aufgehen — to open, swing open (infinitive; separable auf-, of a door)
glossary.brachen: brechen — broke (3rd pl. past); aufbrechen = to break open, prise up
glossary.es: es — it (the child throughout, since das Kind and das Kindlein are neuter; also the impersonal subject, as in „es zwölf Uhr schlug“ = the clock struck twelve)
glossary.fremde: der Fremde — the stranger, the outsider (adj. used as a noun; also fremd ‘strange’)
glossary.gehören: gehören — to belong (infinitive, + dative; „wem es gehören könnte“ = whose it could be)
glossary.graben: graben — to dig (infinitive); not der Graben ‘ditch’
glossary.heller: der Heller — Heller, the smallest old copper coin (acc. pl. here); not the adjective hell
